title: Gambhir Has Lost Ten Tests as India's Coach. The BCCI Looked for an Alternative. There Wasn't One.
excerpt: VVS Laxman was informally approached to take over the Test coaching role, but turned it down. Gambhir's 36 per cent win rate in Tests is the worst by any India coach in the modern era — yet his white-ball record keeps him safe.
body:
Gautam Gambhir stood at the press conference podium in Mullanpur on Thursday evening and said the words he has said before, in Bengaluru, in Guwahati, in Cape Town. "I don't look for excuses." The Afghanistan Test was about to begin. India were at home, in familiar conditions, and heavily favoured. But for Gambhir, every Test match now comes wrapped in a question that will not go away: can this team win red-ball cricket consistently under his coaching?

The numbers say they cannot. Not yet, anyway.

## The Record That Cannot Be Ignored

In 19 Tests as India's head coach, Gambhir has presided over seven wins and ten defeats. His win percentage of 36.84 per cent is the worst by any India coach in the modern era — lower than Ravi Shastri's 60.87 per cent across 46 Tests, and comfortably below Rahul Dravid's 58 per cent across 24. The two draws do little to cushion the fall.

The defeats have not been random or scattered. They follow a pattern that points to systemic issues rather than bad luck. India lost a home series to New Zealand for the first time in over a decade. They were whitewashed 2-0 by South Africa at home just last November. The Border-Gavaskar Trophy, held for over a decade, was surrendered. Not a single away Test series has been won under Gambhir's watch.

"People can keep forgetting, but I'm the same guy who got the results in England," Gambhir said after the South Africa debacle, pointing to India's 2-2 draw in England in 2025. That is true. It is also true that a drawn series away from home is the ceiling of his Test coaching tenure so far.

## The Laxman Approach

Behind the scenes, the BCCI has been quietly exploring alternatives — at least for the red-ball format. According to reports in India Today and CricTracker, VVS Laxman, currently the head of the BCCI's Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru, was informally approached about taking over as India's Test coach in a split-coaching arrangement that would leave Gambhir in charge of ODIs and T20Is.

Laxman, by all accounts, declined. The former Test specialist has spent nearly four years building the Centre of Excellence into one of the most important institutions in Indian cricket and has repeatedly expressed a preference for a role that does not require the relentless travel schedule of a head coach. A board official, quoted by India Today, acknowledged the reality: "There aren't too many alternate options in the red-ball format since VVS Laxman isn't interested in coaching the senior Test team."

This leaves Gambhir in place by default as much as by endorsement — a position that would feel precarious for most coaches, but which Gambhir has navigated with characteristic directness.

## The White-Ball Contrast

What makes the Gambhir debate so unusual is the stark split between his red-ball and white-ball records. In T20 internationals, he has not lost a single series as coach. India won the Champions Trophy and Asia Cup under his watch earlier this year. His T20I win rate stands above 90 per cent. In ODIs, India have won nine of 14, a respectable 64 per cent.

If you only looked at limited-overs cricket, Gambhir would be among the most successful coaches India have ever had. It is the Test record that drags the overall assessment down, and it is the Test record that the BCCI appears most troubled by.

The appointment of Shreyas Iyer as the new T20I captain, announced on Saturday, further stabilises Gambhir's white-ball position. Iyer is seen as Gambhir's pick, a captain who has thrived under franchise pressure and who shares Gambhir's tactical directness. The white-ball future is being built in Gambhir's image.

## The Transition Argument

Gambhir's defence has been consistent: this is a team in transition. Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma have stepped away from Test cricket. R Ashwin retired during the Border-Gavaskar series. Ravindra Jadeja's workload has been managed. The core that dominated Test cricket for a decade is gone, and its replacements — Shubman Gill, Sai Sudharsan, Yashasvi Jaiswal, Dhruv Jurel, Manav Suthar — have played fewer than 30 Tests each.

"We played nine Test matches, did brilliantly in England and then beat the West Indies," Gambhir said on Thursday. "When people talk about transition, that's where it really began."

## What NRIs Are Watching

For diaspora fans in the US, UK, and Canada, the Gambhir coaching saga is more than a cricket story. It is a story about accountability, institutional decision-making, and the tension between loyalty and performance. NRIs who woke up at odd hours to watch India capitulate at home against New Zealand and South Africa are asking a fair question: at what point does transition end and underperformance begin?

The Afghanistan Test, with India piling on runs against a weaker attack, will not answer that question. The Sri Lanka and New Zealand series later this year will. Gambhir knows this. The BCCI knows this. And, apparently, so does VVS Laxman — who chose to say no.
